Họ mời hai mươi khách, nhưng nói với bà đó chỉ là bữa trưa gia đình. Khi bà bước vào, mọi người hô to "Chúc mừng sinh nhật!". Bà bất ngờ đến mức vừa cười vừa khóc. Tuấn tặng bà một món quà: một cuốn album ảnh gia đình. Sau đó bà thổi nến trên bánh.

qs.q: How old was Grandma Huong?
qs.why: “Grandma Huong turned eighty last Sunday, and her family wanted to celebrate with a surprise party.”

qs.q: What did Tuan give his grandmother?
qs.why: “Tuan gave her a gift: a photo book of the family.”

qs.q: Why did they tell Grandma it was just a family lunch?
qs.a: They wanted the party to be a surprise
w: They had no money for a party
qs.why: “They invited twenty guests, but they told Grandma it was just a family lunch.”

items.title: Hung's Big Race
items.text: Hung was very nervous before his first bike race in Da Lat. The road went up and down the mountains, and some parts were really scary. In the middle of the race it started to rain. Hung was scared, but he didn't stop. He thought, "Maybe I'm crazy, but I want to finish!" He came fifth out of forty riders. His coach said, "That was excellent, Hung. Your first race was brilliant!" Hung felt incredible.
items.vi: Hùng rất hồi hộp trước cuộc đua xe đạp đầu tiên ở Đà Lạt. Con đường lên xuống núi, và vài đoạn thật đáng sợ. Giữa cuộc đua trời bắt đầu mưa. Hùng sợ, nhưng anh không dừng lại. Anh nghĩ: "Có lẽ mình điên, nhưng mình muốn về đích!" Anh về thứ năm trong số bốn mươi người đua. Huấn luyện viên nói: "Tuyệt lắm, Hùng. Cuộc đua đầu tiên của em thật xuất sắc!" Hùng thấy thật tuyệt vời.

qs.q: What happened in the middle of the race?
qs.why: “In the middle of the race it started to rain.”

qs.q: What place did Hung finish in?
qs.why: “He came fifth out of forty riders.”

qs.q: How did Hung's coach feel about the race?
qs.why: “His coach said, "That was excellent, Hung. Your first race was brilliant!"”

items.title: Tom Learns to Eat Pho
items.text: Tom came to Hanoi from England last month. On his first morning, his friend Nam took him to a small pho shop. The cook put a big bowl of soup on the table, with a spoon and chopsticks. Next to it was a plate of fresh green vegetables. Tom asked for a fork and a knife, and everyone laughed kindly. Nam showed him how to use chopsticks. Tom added a little hot sauce, and he loved the taste. Now he eats pho three times a week, without a fork!
items.vi: Tom đến Hà Nội từ nước Anh tháng trước. Sáng đầu tiên, bạn anh là Nam đưa anh đến một quán phở nhỏ. Người nấu đặt một bát phở to lên bàn, kèm thìa và đũa. Bên cạnh là một đĩa rau xanh tươi. Tom xin một cái nĩa và một con dao, và mọi người cười thân thiện. Nam chỉ anh cách dùng đũa. Tom cho thêm một chút tương cay, và anh rất thích vị của nó. Bây giờ anh ăn phở ba lần một tuần, không cần nĩa!

qs.q: What did Tom ask for?
qs.why: “Tom asked for a fork and a knife, and everyone laughed kindly.”

qs.q: Who taught Tom to use chopsticks?
qs.why: “Nam showed him how to use chopsticks.”

qs.q: How does Tom feel about pho now?
w: He thinks it is too hot
He only eats it with a fork
qs.why: “Now he eats pho three times a week, without a fork!”

items.title: The Fisherman and the Storm
items.tvi: Người đánh cá và cơn bão
items.text: Mr Ba is a fisherman in a small village on the coast near Quang Ngai. Every morning he looks at the sky before he goes out on the ocean. One day the sky was dark and the wind was very strong. "A storm is coming," he said. He told the other fishermen to stay home. That afternoon the waves were higher than the houses. Everyone was safe because Mr Ba understood the sea.
items.vi: Ông Ba là một ngư dân ở một ngôi làng nhỏ ven biển gần Quảng Ngãi. Mỗi sáng ông nhìn bầu trời trước khi ra khơi. Một hôm trời tối sầm và gió rất mạnh. "Bão sắp đến," ông nói. Ông bảo những ngư dân khác ở nhà. Chiều hôm đó sóng cao hơn cả những ngôi nhà. Mọi người đều an toàn vì ông Ba hiểu biển.

qs.q: What does Mr Ba do every morning?
w: He sells fish at the market
qs.why: “Every morning he looks at the sky before he goes out on the ocean.”

qs.q: What did Mr Ba tell the other fishermen?
qs.why: “He told the other fishermen to stay home.”

qs.q: Why was everyone safe?
qs.a: Mr Ba knew the weather and the sea well
w: The village had a big wall
qs.why: “Everyone was safe because Mr Ba understood the sea.”

items.title: Lan Draws the City
items.text: Lan is an art student in Hanoi. Every Sunday she takes her small notebook and draws old buildings. Last Sunday she drew the red bridge at Hoan Kiem Lake. Then she walked to the big church near the lake and drew its two tall towers. In the afternoon she visited an art gallery and climbed the stairs to the top floor. From the window she could see many roofs. "Next week I will draw the old city gate," she said.
items.vi: Lan là sinh viên mỹ thuật ở Hà Nội. Chủ nhật nào cô cũng mang cuốn sổ nhỏ đi vẽ những toà nhà cổ. Chủ nhật trước, cô vẽ cây cầu đỏ ở hồ Hoàn Kiếm. Sau đó cô đi bộ đến nhà thờ lớn gần hồ và vẽ hai ngọn tháp cao của nó. Buổi chiều, cô ghé một phòng tranh và leo cầu thang lên tầng trên cùng. Từ cửa sổ, cô có thể thấy rất nhiều mái nhà. "Tuần sau mình sẽ vẽ cổng thành cổ," cô nói.

qs.q: What did Lan draw at Hoan Kiem Lake?
qs.why: “Last Sunday she drew the red bridge at Hoan Kiem Lake.”

qs.q: What could she see from the gallery window?
qs.why: “From the window she could see many roofs.”

qs.q: What does Lan enjoy doing?
qs.why: “Every Sunday she takes her small notebook and draws old buildings.”

items.title: Ha's Father Is a Pilot
items.tvi: Bố của Hà là phi công
items.text: Ha's father is a pilot for a Vietnamese airline. He flies big planes from Hanoi to Tokyo and Seoul. He says planes are the fastest transport in the world. Last month he took Ha to work for a day. First they went to the reception desk, and a woman gave Ha a special card. Then her father showed her the front of the plane. Ha sat in the pilot's seat and looked at all the lights. "One day I want to fly too," she said. Her father smiled and pointed towards the sky.
items.vi: Bố của Hà là phi công của một hãng hàng không Việt Nam. Ông lái những chiếc máy bay lớn từ Hà Nội đến Tokyo và Seoul. Ông nói máy bay là phương tiện nhanh nhất thế giới. Tháng trước, bố đưa Hà đi làm cùng một ngày. Đầu tiên họ đến quầy lễ tân, và một cô nhân viên đưa cho Hà một tấm thẻ đặc biệt. Sau đó bố cho cô bé xem buồng lái ở đầu máy bay. Hà ngồi vào ghế phi công và nhìn tất cả những chiếc đèn. "Một ngày nào đó con cũng muốn bay," cô bé nói. Bố cô mỉm cười và chỉ tay lên bầu trời.

qs.q: Where does Ha's father fly?
qs.why: “He flies big planes from Hanoi to Tokyo and Seoul.”

qs.q: What did Ha get at the reception desk?
qs.why: “First they went to the reception desk, and a woman gave Ha a special card.”

qs.q: What job might Ha want in the future?
qs.why: “"One day I want to fly too," she said.”

items.title: Linh at the Pool
items.text: Linh is six, and today is her first time at the swimming pool. She is afraid of the water, so she holds her father's hand very tightly. Her father says, "Don't worry. Jump in, and I will catch you." Linh shakes her head. Her brother wants to push her in, but Dad stops him. Then she sees other children jump and laugh. Slowly she touches the water with her foot. It is warm! Finally she jumps, and her father catches her. Now she doesn't want to leave the pool!
items.vi: Linh sáu tuổi, và hôm nay là lần đầu cô bé đến bể bơi. Cô bé sợ nước, nên nắm tay bố thật chặt. Bố nói: "Đừng lo. Con nhảy xuống đi, bố sẽ đỡ con." Linh lắc đầu. Anh trai muốn đẩy em xuống, nhưng bố ngăn lại. Rồi cô bé thấy những đứa trẻ khác nhảy xuống và cười vui. Cô bé từ từ chạm chân vào nước. Nước ấm! Cuối cùng cô bé nhảy, và bố đỡ được em. Giờ thì cô bé chẳng muốn rời bể bơi nữa!

qs.q: Why does Linh hold her father's hand?
qs.a: She is scared of the water
qs.why: “She is afraid of the water, so she holds her father's hand very tightly.”

qs.q: What does Linh do with her foot?
qs.why: “Slowly she touches the water with her foot.”

qs.q: How does Linh feel at the end?
qs.a: She is happy in the pool
qs.why: “Now she doesn't want to leave the pool!”

items.title: My First Job
items.tvi: Công việc đầu tiên của tôi
items.text:
When I was eighteen, I got my first job in a small bookshop near the station. I worked there every Saturday and Sunday from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon. At first, I was very nervous because I didn't know where the books were, and customers asked me lots of questions. The owner, Mr Hai, was kind and patient. He showed me how to use the computer and how to order new books.
After a few weeks, I started to enjoy the job. I loved talking to people about books, and I often read during my lunch break. The money wasn't very good, but I saved enough to buy my first laptop. I also learned how to be polite to difficult customers.
I stayed at the bookshop for two years, until I went to university in another city. I still visit Mr Hai when I come home, and he always gives me a book as a present.
items.vi:
Năm mười tám tuổi, tôi có công việc đầu tiên ở một hiệu sách nhỏ gần ga. Tôi làm ở đó mỗi thứ Bảy và Chủ nhật, từ chín giờ sáng tới năm giờ chiều. Lúc đầu tôi rất lo vì không biết sách để ở đâu, và khách hỏi rất nhiều. Chủ hiệu, ông Hải, tốt bụng và kiên nhẫn. Ông chỉ tôi cách dùng máy tính và cách đặt sách mới.
Vài tuần sau, tôi bắt đầu thích công việc. Tôi thích nói chuyện với mọi người về sách và hay đọc sách giờ nghỉ trưa. Lương không cao, nhưng tôi để dành đủ tiền mua chiếc máy tính xách tay đầu tiên. Tôi cũng học được cách lịch sự với khách khó tính.
Tôi làm ở hiệu sách hai năm, tới khi đi học đại học ở thành phố khác. Mỗi lần về nhà tôi vẫn ghé thăm ông Hải, và lần nào ông cũng tặng tôi một cuốn sách.

qs.q: When did the writer work at the bookshop?
qs.why: “I worked there every Saturday and Sunday.”

qs.q: Why was the writer nervous at first?
qs.a: He didn't know where things were
qs.why: “I didn't know where the books were.”

qs.q: What did the writer buy with the money?
qs.why: “I saved enough to buy my first laptop.”

qs.q: Why did the writer leave the job?
qs.why: “until I went to university in another city.”

items.title: The Night Market
items.text:
Every Friday and Saturday evening, the main street in our town becomes a night market. Cars can't drive there from six o'clock, and more than a hundred small stalls open. You can buy clothes, shoes, toys and things for the home, but most people come for the food.
My favourite stall sells grilled corn with butter and chilli. It costs only fifteen thousand dong, and there is always a long line. Next to it, an old woman makes sweet soup with beans and coconut milk. She has worked at the market for over twenty years.
The market is also a good place for music. On Saturdays, students from the music school play guitar and sing near the fountain. Tourists often stop to take photos and listen.
The only problem is the rubbish. After the market closes at eleven, the street is very dirty. Now the town has a new plan: every stall must take its rubbish home, and there are more bins on the street.
items.vi:
Mỗi tối thứ Sáu và thứ Bảy, con phố chính của thị trấn tôi thành chợ đêm. Từ sáu giờ xe ô tô không được đi vào, và hơn một trăm sạp nhỏ mở bán. Có thể mua quần áo, giày, đồ chơi và đồ dùng trong nhà, nhưng phần lớn mọi người tới để ăn.
Sạp tôi thích nhất bán ngô nướng bơ và ớt. Giá chỉ mười lăm nghìn đồng và lúc nào cũng có hàng dài. Bên cạnh, một bà cụ nấu chè đậu với nước cốt dừa. Bà đã bán ở chợ hơn hai mươi năm.
Chợ cũng là nơi hay để nghe nhạc. Tối thứ Bảy, sinh viên trường nhạc chơi ghi-ta và hát gần đài phun nước. Khách du lịch hay dừng lại chụp ảnh và nghe.
Vấn đề duy nhất là rác. Sau khi chợ đóng lúc mười một giờ, phố rất bẩn. Giờ thị trấn có kế hoạch mới: sạp nào cũng phải mang rác về, và trên phố có thêm thùng rác.

qs.q: What happens on the main street from six o'clock?
qs.why: “Cars can't drive there from six o'clock.”

qs.q: Why do most people go to the market?
qs.why: “most people come for the food.”

qs.q: Who plays music on Saturdays?
qs.why: “students from the music school play guitar and sing.”

qs.q: What is the town's new plan about?
qs.why: “every stall must take its rubbish home, and there are more bins.”

items.title: Learning to Swim at Thirty
items.tvi: Học bơi năm ba mươi tuổi
items.text:
I never learned to swim when I was a child. My family lived in the city, far from the sea, and there was no swimming pool near our home. When my friends went to the beach, I stayed on the sand and watched them.
Last year, when I was thirty, my daughter started swimming lessons. I felt a little embarrassed because she could swim and I couldn't. So I decided to take lessons too. The teacher, Linh, was younger than me, but she was very good. The first lesson was difficult. I was afraid to put my face in the water, and I drank a lot of it!
Linh told me to relax and practise breathing. I went to the pool three times a week, early in the morning before work. After two months, I could swim twenty-five metres without stopping. Now my daughter and I swim together every Sunday. Next summer, we want to swim in the sea for the first time.
items.vi:
Hồi nhỏ tôi chưa bao giờ học bơi. Nhà tôi ở thành phố, xa biển, và gần nhà không có bể bơi. Khi bạn bè ra biển, tôi ngồi trên cát nhìn họ.
Năm ngoái, khi tôi ba mươi tuổi, con gái tôi bắt đầu học bơi. Tôi hơi ngượng vì con bơi được còn tôi thì không. Thế là tôi quyết định học luôn. Cô giáo, Linh, trẻ hơn tôi nhưng dạy rất giỏi. Buổi đầu rất khó. Tôi sợ úp mặt xuống nước và uống bao nhiêu là nước!
Linh bảo tôi thả lỏng và tập thở. Tôi đi bơi ba buổi một tuần, sáng sớm trước giờ làm. Sau hai tháng, tôi bơi được hai mươi lăm mét không nghỉ. Giờ Chủ nhật nào hai mẹ con cũng bơi cùng nhau. Hè tới, chúng tôi muốn bơi ở biển lần đầu.

qs.q: Why didn't the writer learn to swim as a child?
qs.a: There was no pool or sea near home
qs.why: “far from the sea, and there was no swimming pool near our home.”

qs.q: Why did she decide to take lessons?
qs.why: “she could swim and I couldn't. So I decided to take lessons too.”

qs.q: When did she go to the pool?
qs.why: “early in the morning before work.”

qs.q: What do they want to do next summer?
qs.why: “we want to swim in the sea for the first time.”

items.title: A Message to the New Neighbours
items.text:
Dear new neighbours,
Welcome to Lotus Building! My name is Hoa and I live in flat 5B, just opposite you. I've lived here for six years, so here is some useful information.
The rubbish room is on the ground floor, next to the lift. Please put bottles and paper in the blue bins and food in the green bins. The rubbish is collected every morning at seven.
There is a small supermarket across the road. It opens at six in the morning and closes at ten at night. For fresh fruit and vegetables, the market on Tran Phu Street is better and cheaper, but it closes at noon.
The lift is sometimes broken, usually at the weekend. If it doesn't work, call Mr Tam, the building manager. His number is on the board in the hall.
Finally, every first Sunday of the month we have a building meeting in the garden at four o'clock. Please come and meet everyone!
Best wishes,
Hoa
items.vi:
Gửi các bạn hàng xóm mới,
Chào mừng tới toà nhà Lotus! Tôi là Hoa, ở căn 5B ngay đối diện. Tôi đã sống ở đây sáu năm, nên xin gửi vài thông tin có ích.
Phòng rác ở tầng trệt, cạnh thang máy. Hãy bỏ chai lọ và giấy vào thùng xanh dương, đồ ăn vào thùng xanh lá. Rác được thu mỗi sáng lúc bảy giờ.
Bên kia đường có một siêu thị nhỏ, mở từ sáu giờ sáng tới mười giờ tối. Muốn mua rau quả tươi thì chợ trên phố Trần Phú tốt và rẻ hơn, nhưng đóng cửa lúc trưa.
Thang máy thỉnh thoảng hỏng, thường vào cuối tuần. Nếu thang máy không chạy, hãy gọi ông Tâm, quản lý toà nhà. Số của ông ở bảng tin ở sảnh.
Cuối cùng, Chủ nhật đầu tiên mỗi tháng có họp toà nhà ở vườn lúc bốn giờ. Mời các bạn tới làm quen mọi người!
Chúc mọi điều tốt đẹp,
Hoa

qs.q: Why does Hoa write the message?
qs.a: To give the new neighbours useful information
qs.why: “here is some useful information.”

qs.q: Where should you put old newspapers?
qs.why: “put bottles and paper in the blue bins.”

qs.q: Why is the market better than the supermarket?
qs.why: “the market on Tran Phu Street is better and cheaper.”

qs.q: What should you do if the lift is broken?
w: Use the stairs at the back
qs.why: “call Mr Tam, the building manager.”

items.title: The Bike Trip
items.text:
Last month, my brother and I went on a three-day bike trip in the countryside. We started from our village early on Friday morning with small bags, water and a map.
On the first day, the weather was perfect. We rode sixty kilometres along a river and stopped for lunch in a small restaurant. The owner gave us free bananas and told us about a beautiful waterfall nearby, so we went to see it in the afternoon.
The second day was harder. It rained all morning and the road was muddy. My brother's bike had a flat tyre, and we didn't have the right tools. Luckily, a farmer helped us and fixed it in ten minutes. We stayed that night in a homestay with a friendly family, and we ate dinner together.
On Sunday we rode home slowly. We were tired and dirty, but very happy. We want to do another trip in the dry season, and next time we will bring better tools.
items.vi:
Tháng trước, anh trai tôi và tôi đi xe đạp ba ngày ở vùng quê. Chúng tôi xuất phát từ làng sáng sớm thứ Sáu, mang túi nhỏ, nước và bản đồ.
Ngày đầu trời đẹp tuyệt. Chúng tôi đạp sáu mươi cây số dọc một con sông và dừng ăn trưa ở một quán nhỏ. Chủ quán cho chúng tôi chuối và kể về một thác nước đẹp gần đó, nên buổi chiều chúng tôi đi xem.
Ngày thứ hai vất vả hơn. Mưa cả buổi sáng và đường lầy lội. Xe anh tôi bị xịt lốp mà chúng tôi không mang đúng dụng cụ. May là có một bác nông dân giúp, sửa xong trong mười phút. Tối đó chúng tôi ở homestay với một gia đình thân thiện và cùng ăn tối.
Chủ nhật chúng tôi thong thả đạp về. Mệt và bẩn nhưng rất vui. Chúng tôi muốn đi chuyến nữa vào mùa khô, và lần sau sẽ mang dụng cụ tốt hơn.

qs.why: “a three-day bike trip.”

qs.a: A restaurant owner told them about it
qs.why: “The owner … told us about a beautiful waterfall nearby.”

qs.a: A bike had a flat tyre
qs.why: “My brother's bike had a flat tyre.”

qs.why: “next time we will bring better tools.”

items.title: Online Shopping
items.text:
Many people in Vietnam now buy things online. It is quick and easy: you choose something on your phone, pay by card or pay when it arrives, and a driver brings it to your door, often the next day.
My aunt, who is sixty, started shopping online last year. At first, she only bought small things like soap and rice. Now she buys almost everything online, even clothes and a new fan. She says it saves her time and she doesn't have to carry heavy bags.
But online shopping has problems too. Last month, I ordered a jacket. In the photo it looked dark blue, but when it arrived it was bright purple, and it was too small. Sending it back took two weeks.
My advice is simple. Read what other customers write before you buy, check the size carefully, and buy from shops with good reviews. And for shoes, I still go to a real shop and try them on!
items.vi:
Nhiều người ở Việt Nam giờ mua đồ trên mạng. Nhanh và dễ: chọn món trên điện thoại, trả bằng thẻ hoặc trả khi nhận hàng, và tài xế mang tới tận cửa, thường là hôm sau.
Dì tôi sáu mươi tuổi, năm ngoái bắt đầu mua sắm trên mạng. Lúc đầu dì chỉ mua đồ nhỏ như xà phòng và gạo. Giờ dì mua gần như mọi thứ trên mạng, cả quần áo và một cái quạt mới. Dì bảo vừa tiết kiệm thời gian vừa không phải xách túi nặng.
Nhưng mua trên mạng cũng có vấn đề. Tháng trước tôi đặt một chiếc áo khoác. Trong ảnh trông màu xanh đậm, nhưng khi nhận thì màu tím sáng, lại còn chật. Gửi trả mất hai tuần.
Lời khuyên của tôi đơn giản. Đọc khách khác viết gì trước khi mua, xem kỹ cỡ, và mua ở cửa hàng được đánh giá tốt. Còn giày thì tôi vẫn ra cửa hàng thật để thử!

qs.why: “At first, she only bought small things like soap and rice.”

qs.a: It saves time and she doesn't carry heavy bags
qs.why: “it saves her time and she doesn't have to carry heavy bags.”

qs.why: “it was bright purple, and it was too small.”

qs.why: “I still go to a real shop and try them on!”

items.title: The Cooking Class
items.text:
For my birthday, my friends gave me a ticket for a cooking class in the old town. The class was on a Thursday evening and there were eight students from five different countries.
Our teacher, Chef Minh, started by taking us to the market. He showed us how to choose fresh fish and herbs, and he taught us the Vietnamese names of some vegetables. Then we walked back to his kitchen, which was on the second floor of an old yellow house.
We cooked three dishes: spring rolls, sour fish soup and a mango dessert. The spring rolls were the hardest because the rice paper broke easily. My first two were terrible, but the third one was perfect! The soup was easier, and everyone loved the dessert.
At the end, we sat at a long table and ate everything together. Chef Minh gave us the recipes on cards to take home. Last weekend, I cooked the soup for my family, and my dad asked for more.
items.vi:
Sinh nhật tôi, bạn bè tặng vé một lớp học nấu ăn ở phố cổ. Lớp vào tối thứ Năm, có tám học viên từ năm nước khác nhau.
Thầy, đầu bếp Minh, bắt đầu bằng việc dẫn chúng tôi đi chợ. Thầy chỉ cách chọn cá tươi và rau thơm, và dạy tên tiếng Việt của vài loại rau. Rồi chúng tôi đi bộ về bếp của thầy, ở tầng hai một ngôi nhà cũ màu vàng.
Chúng tôi nấu ba món: nem cuốn, canh chua cá và món tráng miệng xoài. Nem khó nhất vì bánh tráng dễ rách. Hai cái đầu của tôi tệ lắm, nhưng cái thứ ba thì hoàn hảo! Canh dễ hơn, và ai cũng mê món tráng miệng.
Cuối buổi, chúng tôi ngồi một bàn dài ăn hết mọi thứ cùng nhau. Thầy Minh tặng công thức in trên thẻ để mang về. Cuối tuần trước, tôi nấu canh cho cả nhà, và bố tôi xin thêm.

qs.why: “my friends gave me a ticket.”

qs.q: What did they do first?
qs.why: “Chef Minh started by taking us to the market.”

qs.q: Which dish was the most difficult?
qs.why: “The spring rolls were the hardest.”

qs.q: What did the writer's father think of the soup?
qs.why: “my dad asked for more.”

items.title: A Volunteer Weekend
items.text:
Every year, our university organises a volunteer weekend in a mountain village. This year, twenty students went, and I was one of them. We travelled for seven hours by bus and arrived late on Friday night.
On Saturday morning, we painted the walls of the village school. The old paint was grey and dirty, so we chose bright colours: yellow, green and orange. In the afternoon, some students taught English songs to the children, and others helped the teachers fix tables and chairs.
The children were shy at first, but soon they laughed and sang with us. A girl called Pa gave me a bracelet she made from coloured thread. I still wear it every day.
On Sunday, the village families cooked a big lunch for us before we left. The food was simple but delicious. On the bus home, nobody talked much. We were tired, but we all felt that it was the best weekend of the year.
items.vi:
Năm nào trường đại học của chúng tôi cũng tổ chức một cuối tuần tình nguyện ở một bản vùng núi. Năm nay có hai mươi sinh viên đi, trong đó có tôi. Chúng tôi đi xe khách bảy tiếng, tới nơi khuya tối thứ Sáu.
Sáng thứ Bảy, chúng tôi sơn tường trường học của bản. Lớp sơn cũ xám và bẩn, nên chúng tôi chọn màu tươi: vàng, xanh lá và cam. Buổi chiều, vài bạn dạy bọn trẻ hát tiếng Anh, số khác giúp thầy cô sửa bàn ghế.
Bọn trẻ lúc đầu ngại, nhưng chẳng mấy chốc đã cười và hát cùng chúng tôi. Một bé gái tên Pa tặng tôi chiếc vòng tay em tự làm bằng chỉ màu. Tôi vẫn đeo nó hằng ngày.
Chủ nhật, các gia đình trong bản nấu một bữa trưa lớn cho chúng tôi trước khi về. Đồ ăn đơn giản mà ngon. Trên xe về, chẳng ai nói nhiều. Ai cũng mệt, nhưng đều thấy đó là cuối tuần tuyệt nhất trong năm.

qs.why: “We travelled for seven hours by bus.”

items.title: Working from Home
items.text:
When Hoa's company let staff work from home two days a week, she was delighted. She would save an hour of travel every day and could finally have breakfast with her children.
The first month was not as easy as she had expected. Her flat was small, so she had to work at the kitchen table. Her neighbours were building a new bathroom, and the noise made phone meetings difficult. She also noticed that she was working longer hours, because there was no clear moment when the day ended.
So Hoa made some changes. She bought a small desk and put it in the corner of the bedroom. She started every home day by getting dressed as if she were going to the office, and she turned her computer off at six o'clock exactly. On Fridays she went to a café near her flat for two hours, just to see other people.
Now, she says, home days are her most productive. "The secret," she explains, "is to treat home like an office, but not to let the office take over your home."

qs.a: Her flat was small and noisy, and she worked too long
w: Her children were at home all day
Her company asked her to come back

qs.q: What does Hoa do at six o'clock?
qs.why: “she turned her computer off at six o'clock exactly.”

qs.q: What is Hoa's advice?
qs.a: Keep work and home life separate
w: Work in a café every day
Don't work from home at all
qs.why: “treat home like an office, but not to let the office take over your home.”

items.title: A Message from the Sports Centre

items.title: The Boy Who Fixed Bicycles
items.text:
When Tuan was twelve, his bicycle broke on the way to school. His family had no money for a new one, so he took it apart in the yard and tried to repair it himself. It took him three weekends, and he made many mistakes, but in the end it worked.
Soon his neighbours began bringing him their broken bikes. At first he did it for free, but his grandmother told him that his time had value. He started charging a small amount and saved every coin in a tin box.
By the time he was sixteen, Tuan had saved enough to rent a tiny space at the market. He painted a sign that said 'Tuan's Bikes' and worked there every afternoon after school. His teachers were worried that he would fall behind, but his marks actually improved, because he had learned to plan his time carefully.
Today Tuan is twenty-five and owns two shops. He still keeps the old tin box on his desk. "It reminds me," he says, "that every big thing starts with something small."

qs.a: His family couldn't afford a new one

qs.why: “His family had no money for a new one.”

qs.a: That he should be paid for his work
qs.why: “his grandmother told him that his time had value. He started charging…”

qs.q: What happened to his school marks?
qs.why: “his marks actually improved.”

items.title: Should Students Wear Uniforms?
items.tvi: Học sinh có nên mặc đồng phục?
items.text:
Last week our school asked students what they thought about uniforms. Here are two opinions.
Linh, 15: "I'm in favour of uniforms. In the morning I don't have to think about what to wear, so I save time. Also, nobody can see whose family is rich and whose family is poor, so there is less pressure. Some people say uniforms are boring, but we can still show our personality with our bags, hair and shoes."
Khang, 16: "I disagree. Uniforms are expensive, because we have to buy them from the school shop and they don't last long. They are also uncomfortable in hot weather. I think we should be allowed to wear our own clothes, with a few simple rules, for example no very short skirts or offensive slogans. Learning how to dress well is part of growing up."
The head teacher says the school will make a decision next month after talking to parents.

qs.q: According to Linh, why do uniforms reduce pressure?
qs.a: Students can't see who is rich or poor
w: Students don't need to buy bags
qs.why: “nobody can see whose family is rich and whose family is poor, so there is less pressure.”

qs.q: What does Khang say about the price of uniforms?
qs.a: They cost a lot and wear out quickly
w: They are cheaper than normal clothes
qs.why: “Uniforms are expensive… they don't last long.”

qs.q: What will happen next?
qs.a: The school will decide after talking to parents
qs.why: “the school will make a decision next month after talking to parents.”

items.title: My First Job Interview
items.tvi: Buổi phỏng vấn xin việc đầu tiên
items.text:
I had my first job interview last Tuesday, for a part-time position at a bookshop. I was so nervous that I couldn't eat breakfast. I arrived twenty minutes early, which was a good idea, because I got lost inside the shopping centre and found the shop with only five minutes to spare.
The manager, Mrs Ha, was friendly. She asked me why I wanted the job and what books I liked. I had prepared answers to these questions, so I felt more relaxed. Then she asked me something I hadn't expected: "Tell me about a time when you made a mistake." My mind went blank for a few seconds. Then I told her about a group project at school where I forgot to send an important file, and explained how I now write everything in a planner.
At the end, she showed me around the shop and introduced me to two of the staff. Yesterday she phoned to offer me the job. She said that my answer about the mistake was the reason she chose me, because it showed I could learn from problems.

qs.q: Why was it good that the writer arrived early?
qs.a: The writer got lost before finding the shop
qs.why: “I got lost inside the shopping centre and found the shop with only five minutes to spare.”

qs.q: Which question surprised the writer?
qs.a: A question about a mistake they had made
qs.why: “she asked me something I hadn't expected: Tell me about a time when you made a mistake.”

qs.q: Why did Mrs Ha choose the writer?
qs.a: The writer showed they could learn from problems
w: The writer knew a lot about books
The writer was the first to arrive
qs.why: “it showed I could learn from problems.”

items.title: Plastic in the Sea
items.text:
Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic end up in the oceans. Much of it comes from rivers, which carry rubbish from cities to the sea. Once it is in the water, plastic does not disappear. Sunlight and waves break it into very small pieces, called microplastics, which fish and birds eat by mistake.
Scientists have found microplastics in salt, in tap water and even in the air. They are still studying what this means for human health, but many experts believe we should act now rather than wait for the results.
There are some simple things everyone can do. Carrying a reusable bottle and bag is a good start. Saying no to plastic straws and choosing products with less packaging also helps. In some cities, shops give a small discount to customers who bring their own containers.
Governments have a role too. Several countries have banned single-use plastic bags, and a few have introduced deposit schemes, where people get money back when they return bottles. In places where these schemes exist, far fewer bottles are found on beaches.

w: Ships throw it into the water
qs.why: “Much of it comes from rivers, which carry rubbish from cities to the sea.”

qs.q: What do experts think we should do about health risks?
qs.a: Act now without waiting for results
w: Wait until the studies are finished
qs.why: “many experts believe we should act now rather than wait for the results.”

qs.q: What happens where deposit schemes exist?
qs.a: There are fewer bottles on beaches
qs.why: “far fewer bottles are found on beaches.”

items.title: The Night Market Cook
items.tvi: Người nấu ăn ở chợ đêm
items.text:
Mrs Lan has sold noodle soup at the same night market for thirty years. She starts preparing at two in the afternoon, cooking the broth slowly with beef bones, onions and spices. By six o'clock, when the market opens, there is already a queue at her stall.
Many customers are regulars who have been eating there since they were children. Others are tourists who have read about her online. A food blogger wrote about her soup five years ago, and since then visitors from Korea, Australia and France have come to try it. Mrs Lan does not speak much English, but she has learned to say "spicy?" and "one more?" with a big smile.
Last year a restaurant group offered her a job as head cook in their new restaurant in the city centre. The salary was good and she would work in a modern kitchen. She refused. "At the market I can talk to my customers and see their faces when they taste the soup," she says. "In a big kitchen I would just be a name on a menu."
Her daughter now helps her at weekends and is slowly learning the recipe, which has never been written down.

qs.q: Why do many tourists visit Mrs Lan's stall?
qs.a: A blogger wrote about her soup
w: Her stall is in a hotel
qs.why: “A food blogger wrote about her soup five years ago, and since then visitors… have come.”

qs.q: Why did Mrs Lan refuse the restaurant job?
qs.a: She wanted to keep contact with her customers
qs.why: “At the market I can talk to my customers and see their faces.”

qs.q: What do we learn about the recipe?
qs.a: It exists only in Mrs Lan's memory
w: It is printed on the menu
qs.why: “the recipe, which has never been written down.”

items.title: Volunteers Wanted
items.text:
Are you free on Saturday mornings? Do you enjoy working with children? Sunflower Library is looking for volunteers to help with our weekend reading club.
The club is for children aged six to ten who find reading difficult. Volunteers read stories with small groups, play word games and help the children choose books to borrow. You don't need to be a teacher, but you should be patient, friendly and able to read clearly. All volunteers receive a two-hour training session before they start.
We ask volunteers to come at least twice a month for six months, because the children feel more confident when they see the same faces. Sessions run from 8.30 to 11.00, and we provide free drinks and snacks.
Last year, eighty percent of the children in the club improved their reading level by at least one grade. Many parents told us their children now read at home for fun.
To apply, fill in the form on our website before 15 August. We will invite you for a short chat, and training begins on 1 September.

qs.a: Children who have problems with reading

items.title: Learning to Drive at Forty
items.tvi: Học lái xe ở tuổi bốn mươi
items.text:
For most of my life I relied on buses, taxis and my husband to get around. I always told myself I was too nervous to drive. But when we moved to a small town where buses run only twice a day, I realised I had no choice.
My first lesson was terrible. I stopped the engine five times and drove round a roundabout twice because I was too scared to leave it. My instructor, a calm man called Duc, simply laughed and said, "Everyone does that."
What helped me most was practising in a quiet car park on Sunday mornings with my son, who had passed his test the year before. He was surprisingly patient, which was funny, since I had taught him to ride a bike years earlier.
I failed my first driving test because I forgot to check my mirror before turning. I was disappointed, but I booked another test immediately. Six weeks later I passed. Now I drive to work every day, and last month I drove my mother to the coast for her birthday. The independence is wonderful. I only wish I had started twenty years earlier.

qs.q: Why did the writer decide to learn to drive?
qs.a: Public transport in her new town was very limited
w: Her son needed a lift to school
qs.why: “we moved to a small town where buses run only twice a day.”

qs.q: Why does the writer find her son's patience funny?
qs.a: She had once taught him to ride a bike
qs.why: “which was funny, since I had taught him to ride a bike years earlier.”

qs.q: How does the writer feel now?
qs.a: She enjoys her independence but regrets starting late
w: She is still afraid of driving
qs.why: “The independence is wonderful. I only wish I had started twenty years earlier.”

items.title: Review: The Lighthouse Café
items.tvi: Nhận xét: quán cà phê Ngọn Hải Đăng
items.text:
The Lighthouse Café opened in March in an old fishing house next to the harbour. The owners have kept the original wooden walls and decorated them with old maps and photos of local fishermen, which gives the place a warm, relaxed feeling.
I visited on a Wednesday afternoon. The menu is short but interesting, with local seafood, salads and homemade cakes. I had the grilled fish with lemon rice, which was fresh and perfectly cooked, although the portion was quite small for the price. My friend's coconut cake, on the other hand, was huge and delicious.
Service was friendly but slow. We waited almost twenty minutes for our drinks, and the waiter apologised, explaining that two staff members were ill. Still, I would recommend booking a table at weekends, because the terrace with its sea view fills up quickly.
Overall, the Lighthouse Café is a lovely spot for a long, relaxed lunch rather than a quick meal. Go for the view and the cakes, and don't be in a hurry.

qs.a: It was good but too small for the price
w: It was the biggest dish on the menu
qs.why: “fresh and perfectly cooked, although the portion was quite small for the price.”

qs.q: Why was the service slow that day?
qs.why: “two staff members were ill.”

qs.q: Who would enjoy this café most?
qs.a: People who want a long, relaxed meal
w: People who need a quick lunch
People who want a large menu
qs.why: “a lovely spot for a long, relaxed lunch rather than a quick meal.”

items.title: The Four-Day Week
items.text:
When a software company in Da Nang announced that its staff would work four days a week for the same salary, many people assumed productivity would fall. Six months later, the results suggest the opposite.
According to the company's figures, the amount of work completed per week has stayed roughly the same, while sick days have dropped by almost a third. Staff report that they are less tired and spend fewer hours in unnecessary meetings. "When you know you only have four days, you stop wasting time," says project manager Thu Trang. "We cancelled half our regular meetings and nobody missed them."
Not everyone is convinced, however. Some customers have complained that it is harder to reach the company on Fridays, and the firm has had to introduce a rota so that a small team is always available. A few employees also admit that the longer working days can be exhausting, particularly for parents who have to collect children from school.
Economists point out that the model may suit office-based businesses better than hospitals, shops or factories, where work cannot simply be done faster. Even so, the experiment has sparked a lively debate. Several other firms in the city are now running their own trials, and the company's director says she has no intention of going back. "People are not machines," she argues. "If they come back on Monday rested, they do better work. It's that simple."

qs.q: What happened to the number of sick days?
qs.a: It fell by nearly a third
qs.why: “sick days have dropped by almost a third.”

qs.q: Why did the company introduce a rota?
qs.a: So customers could still contact them on Fridays
w: So staff could attend more meetings
qs.why: “harder to reach the company on Fridays… a small team is always available.”

qs.q: What do economists suggest?
qs.a: The model may not work in every kind of business
w: The model should be made law
qs.why: “the model may suit office-based businesses better than hospitals, shops or factories.”

items.title: Why We Forget Names
items.tvi: Vì sao ta hay quên tên
items.text:
Most of us have experienced it: you are introduced to someone, you shake hands, and ten seconds later their name has completely disappeared. It is embarrassing, but psychologists say it is also entirely normal.
The main reason, they explain, is attention. When we meet someone new, our brains are busy with many other things at once: what the person looks like, what we are going to say, whether we are making a good impression. The name is mentioned only once, often quickly, and it simply never gets stored properly. In other words, we don't forget names; we never learn them in the first place.
Names are also unusually difficult to remember because they are arbitrary. If someone tells you they are a baker, the word connects to lots of things you already know: bread, early mornings, the smell of an oven. A name like 'Hung' or 'Sarah', on the other hand, gives the brain very little to hold on to.
Fortunately, there are simple techniques that help. Repeating the name immediately — "Nice to meet you, Hung" — gives your brain a second chance to record it. Linking the name to an image or to someone else you know with the same name also makes it more memorable. Finally, using the name once more at the end of the conversation can fix it in your memory.
None of these tricks is perfect, but they work far better than the most common strategy, which is hoping for the best.

qs.q: According to psychologists, why do we lose names so quickly?
qs.a: We are not paying full attention when we hear them
w: Our memory gets worse with age
qs.why: “The main reason, they explain, is attention… it simply never gets stored properly.”

qs.q: Why is a job easier to remember than a name?
qs.a: It connects to things we already know
qs.why: “the word connects to lots of things you already know… A name… gives the brain very little to hold on to.”

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude to 'hoping for the best'?
qs.a: It is less effective than the techniques described
w: It is the most reliable strategy
qs.why: “they work far better than the most common strategy, which is hoping for the best.”

items.title: Gap Year: Waste of Time or Life Lesson?
items.tvi: Năm nghỉ trước đại học: phí thời gian hay bài học?
items.text:
After finishing school, Minh Anh surprised her parents by announcing that she would not start university immediately. Instead, she wanted to spend a year working and travelling. Her father was horrified. "He was sure I would never go back to studying," she remembers.
She spent the first six months working in a hotel in Hoi An, saving most of her salary. The job was hard: long shifts, difficult guests, and a manager who rarely said thank you. But she learned to deal with complaints calmly and discovered she was good at solving problems under pressure.
With her savings, she then travelled through Laos and Cambodia, volunteering at a school for two months. Teaching children with almost no resources, she says, taught her more about creativity than any classroom ever had.
Critics of gap years argue that they are a luxury for the wealthy and that students lose their study habits. There is some truth in this: a gap year that consists mainly of parties on a beach is unlikely to be valuable. Universities, however, report that students who take a well-planned year out tend to be more motivated and are less likely to drop out.
Minh Anh is now in her second year of a business degree. Her grades are among the best in her class, and her father has changed his mind. "He tells everyone it was his idea," she laughs.

qs.q: What did Minh Anh learn from her hotel job?
qs.a: How to handle problems when under pressure
w: How to save money while travelling
qs.why: “she learned to deal with complaints calmly and discovered she was good at solving problems under pressure.”

qs.q: What does the writer accept about critics' views?
qs.a: A gap year without a plan may have little value
w: Gap years always cause students to drop out
Only rich students should take a gap year
qs.why: “a gap year that consists mainly of parties on a beach is unlikely to be valuable.”

qs.q: What does the last paragraph tell us about her father?
qs.a: He now feels positive about her decision
w: He still disagrees with her choice
qs.why: “her father has changed his mind. He tells everyone it was his idea.”

items.title: The Return of Board Games
items.tvi: Trò chơi bàn cờ trở lại
items.text:
In an age of smartphones and online games, you might expect board games to be disappearing. In fact, the opposite is happening. Sales have grown steadily for over a decade, and board game cafés, where customers pay a small fee to play from a library of hundreds of games, have opened in cities from Seoul to Ho Chi Minh City.
So what explains their popularity? Part of the answer lies in a desire for real-life contact. Many young people spend their working days in front of screens, and sitting around a table with friends offers a welcome break. Unlike online games, board games require players to look at each other, negotiate and laugh together.
The games themselves have also changed. Modern designers have moved away from simple luck-based games towards ones that reward planning and cooperation. In some popular titles, players work together against the game rather than against each other, which makes them attractive to people who dislike competition.
The internet has, ironically, helped too. Online videos explaining the rules make it easy to learn complicated games, and crowdfunding websites allow small designers to raise money without the support of a big company.
Café owner Quang believes the trend will last. "People don't come here just to play," he says. "They come to spend time with people they care about. That never goes out of fashion."

qs.q: What is surprising about board games today, according to the writer?
qs.a: They are becoming more popular despite technology
w: They are cheaper than ever before
qs.why: “you might expect board games to be disappearing. In fact, the opposite is happening.”

qs.q: Why might people who dislike competition enjoy modern games?
qs.a: Some games are played as a team against the game
w: The games depend mostly on luck
qs.why: “players work together against the game rather than against each other.”

qs.q: Why does the writer describe the internet's role as ironic?
qs.a: Technology is helping a non-digital hobby
w: Online games have become less popular
The internet makes rules more complicated
qs.why: “The internet has, ironically, helped too.” (công nghệ giúp trò chơi không dùng màn hình)

items.title: Letter to the Editor: Our Disappearing Trees
items.tvi: Thư gửi toà soạn: cây xanh đang biến mất
items.text:
Dear Editor,
I am writing to express my concern about the number of old trees being cut down in our city centre. In the last year alone, at least forty mature trees have been removed from Tran Phu Street to make room for wider pavements and new shops.
The council claims that the trees were unsafe and that new ones will be planted. While I understand that some old trees can be dangerous in storms, I find it hard to believe that every single one was a risk. Moreover, a young tree takes twenty or thirty years to provide the same shade as the ones we have lost.
The consequences are already obvious. Walking along Tran Phu Street at midday in summer is now extremely unpleasant, and several shopkeepers have told me that fewer customers stop there. Studies from other cities show that streets with trees can be several degrees cooler than those without.
I would like to suggest that the council publish an independent report before removing any more trees, and that residents be consulted. I would also urge readers who share my concern to attend the public meeting at the town hall on 12 May.
Yours faithfully,
Nguyen Van Binh

qs.q: What is the council's explanation for cutting the trees?
w: The trees were too expensive to maintain
qs.why: “The council claims that the trees were unsafe.”

qs.q: Why is the writer not satisfied with planting new trees?
qs.a: New trees take decades to give the same shade
w: There is no space for new trees
qs.why: “a young tree takes twenty or thirty years to provide the same shade.”

qs.q: What does the writer want the council to do?
qs.a: Get an independent report and ask residents' opinions
qs.why: “publish an independent report… and that residents be consulted.”

items.title: Sleep and Teenagers
items.tvi: Giấc ngủ và tuổi mới lớn
items.text:
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up late and then refuse to get out of bed in the morning. It is tempting to blame laziness or phones, but scientists say biology plays a major part.
During adolescence, the body releases melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, about two hours later than it does in children or adults. As a result, many teenagers genuinely cannot fall asleep before eleven or midnight. Since they still need eight to ten hours of sleep, waking up at six for school leaves them seriously short of rest.
The effects of this are not trivial. Research links lack of sleep in young people to poorer concentration, lower exam results, and even a higher risk of road accidents among new drivers. Some studies also suggest a connection with anxiety and depression.
In response, a number of schools in the United States and Europe have experimented with later start times. One district that moved its school day from 7.30 to 8.30 reported better attendance and a noticeable rise in grades. Not all schools find it easy, though: later starts can cause problems with bus timetables and with parents' working hours.
Phones are not completely innocent, of course. The blue light from screens can delay sleep even further. Experts recommend switching devices off an hour before bed — advice that, admittedly, many adults also ignore.

qs.q: According to scientists, why do teenagers go to bed late?
qs.a: Their bodies produce the sleep hormone later
qs.why: “the body releases melatonin… about two hours later.”

qs.q: What happened in the district that started school later?
w: Students went to bed even later
qs.why: “reported better attendance and a noticeable rise in grades.”

qs.q: What does the writer suggest in the last sentence?
qs.a: Adults also don't follow the advice about screens
w: Adults need more sleep than teenagers
Phones are not a real problem
qs.why: “advice that, admittedly, many adults also ignore.”

items.title: The Village That Saved Its School
items.text:
Three years ago, the primary school in the mountain village of Ta Van was about to close. Young families had been moving to the city for work, and the number of pupils had fallen from eighty to just nineteen. The education department argued that it made more sense to send the remaining children by bus to a larger school forty minutes away.
Local people were determined to prevent this. "If the school closes, the village dies," said Mr Sung, whose grandchildren studied there. Residents formed a committee and came up with an unusual plan: they would turn the school into a centre that also served visitors.
With help from a charity, they converted an empty classroom into a small guesthouse. Tourists who stay there pay a fee that goes towards teachers' salaries, and in the afternoons the children practise their English by showing guests around the village. Parents, meanwhile, run cooking and weaving classes for visitors.
The results have exceeded expectations. Pupil numbers have risen to thirty-five, partly because two families moved back after finding work in tourism. The children's English has improved dramatically, and the school has won a regional award for innovation.
There are challenges. Some residents worry that too many tourists could change village life, and the committee now limits the number of guests to six per night. But for now, the school bell still rings every morning — something that seemed impossible three years ago.

qs.q: Why did the education department want to close the school?
qs.a: There were very few pupils left
qs.why: “the number of pupils had fallen from eighty to just nineteen.”

qs.q: How does the guesthouse help the school?
w: It provides classrooms for more pupils
qs.why: “Tourists who stay there pay a fee that goes towards teachers' salaries.”

qs.q: Why does the committee limit the number of guests?
w: The guesthouse has only one room
The children cannot speak enough English
qs.why: “Some residents worry that too many tourists could change village life.”

items.title: Do We Really Need to Own a Car?
items.tvi: Ta có thật cần sở hữu ô tô?
items.text:
For previous generations, buying a car was a symbol of success. Today, a growing number of young city dwellers are deciding that it is simply not worth it.
The arguments are largely financial. Once you add up insurance, fuel, parking, repairs and the loss of value over time, owning a car in a big city can cost far more than people realise. A recent survey found that the average urban car is parked for about 95 percent of its life. Meanwhile, ride-hailing apps, car-sharing schemes and improved public transport mean that it is easier than ever to get around without one.
Environmental concerns also play a role, though perhaps a smaller one than is often claimed. When asked why they had not bought a car, only a quarter of respondents mentioned pollution, compared with more than half who mentioned cost.
Car manufacturers are paying attention. Several now offer monthly subscriptions, allowing customers to use a vehicle without buying it and to change models whenever they like. Others are investing in car-sharing businesses themselves.
Of course, the picture looks very different outside the cities. In rural areas, where buses are rare and distances long, a car or motorbike remains a necessity rather than a choice. The trend away from ownership, therefore, may say more about how cities are changing than about a change in people's values.

qs.q: What was the main reason people gave for not buying a car?
qs.why: “only a quarter… mentioned pollution, compared with more than half who mentioned cost.”

qs.q: How are some car companies responding?
qs.a: By offering cars on monthly subscriptions
w: By lowering the price of new cars
qs.why: “Several now offer monthly subscriptions.”

qs.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
qs.a: The trend reflects changes in cities more than in values
w: Everyone will stop owning cars soon
People in the countryside care more about cars
qs.why: “may say more about how cities are changing than about a change in people's values.”

items.title: Learning from Failure
items.text:
When engineer Pham Duc Long's first business went bankrupt in 2015, he felt ashamed. He had borrowed money from relatives, hired twelve people and promised investors rapid growth. Within two years, everything had gone. "I didn't leave the house for weeks," he admits. "I thought everyone was talking about me."
It was a conversation with an older businesswoman that changed his perspective. She told him that she had failed three times before her current company succeeded, and that each failure had taught her something she could never have learned from a book. She encouraged him to write down exactly what had gone wrong.
The list was painful but useful. Long realised that he had spent too much money on an expensive office before he had enough customers, and that he had ignored early warnings from his accountant because he did not want to hear bad news. Above all, he had never properly tested whether people actually wanted his product.
His second company, launched in 2018, started from his kitchen. He spent six months talking to potential customers before building anything. Today it employs sixty people and is profitable.
Long now gives talks at universities about failure. Students, he says, are often surprised that he talks more about his first company than his second. "Success teaches you very little," he tells them. "Failure, if you are honest about it, teaches you everything."

qs.q: How did Long feel immediately after his first business failed?
qs.a: Embarrassed and unwilling to go out
w: Relieved and full of new ideas
qs.why: “he felt ashamed… I didn't leave the house for weeks.”

qs.q: Which mistake did Long identify?
qs.a: He didn't check if customers wanted the product
w: He listened too much to his accountant
qs.why: “he had never properly tested whether people actually wanted his product.”

qs.q: Why are students surprised by Long's talks?
qs.a: He focuses on his failed company
qs.why: “he talks more about his first company than his second.”

items.title: Street Food Goes Upmarket
items.tvi: Món ăn đường phố lên đời
items.text:
Not long ago, the idea of paying restaurant prices for a bowl of street food would have seemed ridiculous to most Vietnamese diners. Now, in several major cities, chefs are taking dishes traditionally sold from plastic stools on the pavement and serving them in elegant dining rooms at five times the price.
Supporters say this is a way of showing respect for traditional cooking. Chef Mai Linh, whose restaurant serves a refined version of banh xeo, argues that street food has always been undervalued. "These recipes are as complex as anything in French cuisine," she says. "Why shouldn't they be presented with the same care?" She also points out that she buys ingredients from small local farmers and pays her staff well above the average wage.
Critics are less enthusiastic. Food writer Tran Hai believes that something important is lost when street food moves indoors. "Part of the experience is the noise, the crowd, the woman who has cooked the same dish for forty years," he says. "Put it on a white plate and it becomes something else." Others worry that rising prices could eventually push ordinary vendors out of business.
The debate is unlikely to be settled soon. What is clear is that the two worlds can exist side by side. On the street outside Mai Linh's restaurant, a vendor still sells banh xeo for a fraction of the price — and on most evenings, her queue is just as long.

qs.q: Why does Chef Mai Linh think street food deserves careful presentation?
qs.a: Its recipes are just as complex as other cuisines
qs.why: “These recipes are as complex as anything in French cuisine.”

qs.q: What is Tran Hai's main concern?
qs.a: The atmosphere of eating on the street is lost
w: The food in restaurants is less fresh
qs.why: “Part of the experience is the noise, the crowd… Put it on a white plate and it becomes something else.”

qs.q: What does the last paragraph suggest?
qs.a: Street vendors and upmarket restaurants can both succeed
qs.why: “the two worlds can exist side by side… her queue is just as long.”

items.title: The Myth of Multitasking
items.tvi: Ảo tưởng làm nhiều việc cùng lúc
items.text:
Few claims are made with more confidence in job interviews than "I'm good at multitasking." Yet a substantial body of research suggests that, for most tasks, genuine multitasking is something the human brain is simply not built to do.
What we experience as doing two things at once is usually rapid switching between them. Each switch carries a cost: the brain must disengage from one set of rules and reload another, a process that takes a fraction of a second but adds up over a day. Studies have found that people who constantly alternate between email, messaging and a main task can take up to forty percent longer to finish, and make significantly more errors, than those who work on one thing at a time.
Perhaps more strikingly, heavy multitaskers often perform worse even when they are asked to focus on a single task. One well-known experiment found that people who habitually juggled several media streams were more easily distracted by irrelevant information, as though their capacity to filter had been weakened through lack of use.
There are exceptions. Combining a highly automatic activity, such as walking, with a demanding one, such as conversation, causes little difficulty. The problem arises when two activities compete for the same mental resources — reading and listening to speech, for instance, or writing an email during a meeting.
None of this means that modern workplaces will abandon their open-plan offices and endless notifications. But it does suggest that the most productive skill may not be the ability to do everything at once, but the discipline to do one thing properly.

qs.q: What does the writer say really happens when we 'multitask'?
qs.a: We switch quickly between tasks, which costs time
w: We use two separate parts of the brain
We complete tasks faster but less carefully
qs.why: “What we experience as doing two things at once is usually rapid switching between them. Each switch carries a cost.”

qs.q: What did the experiment suggest about habitual multitaskers?
qs.a: They became worse at ignoring distractions
w: They were better at single tasks
They could filter information more quickly
qs.why: “were more easily distracted by irrelevant information.”

qs.q: When is doing two things together NOT a problem?
qs.why: “Combining a highly automatic activity, such as walking, with a demanding one… causes little difficulty.”

qs.q: What is the writer's overall view?
qs.a: Focusing on one thing is more valuable than multitasking
w: Multitasking can be learned through practice
qs.why: “the most productive skill may not be the ability to do everything at once, but the discipline to do one thing properly.”

items.title: Who Owns a City's Pavements?
items.tvi: Vỉa hè thành phố thuộc về ai?
items.text:
Walk along almost any street in Hanoi and you will see the pavement put to a remarkable variety of uses: parked motorbikes, street vendors, families eating dinner on plastic stools, men playing chess, the occasional pedestrian forced to step into the road. To foreign visitors this can seem chaotic; to many residents it is simply how a city should work.
Periodic campaigns to 'reclaim the pavement' for walkers have produced mixed results. Officials argue that clear pavements are safer and make the city more attractive to tourists and investors. Critics counter that such campaigns tend to target the poorest — vendors who depend on the street for their living — while leaving untouched the cafés and car showrooms that occupy far larger areas.
Urban planners increasingly argue that the question is framed wrongly. Rather than asking whether pavements should be for walking or for trade, they suggest asking how both can coexist. Some cities have experimented with marked zones: a strip reserved for pedestrians, with vending permitted alongside it at certain hours. Others have widened pavements on busy routes while removing parking spaces, a move that is invariably unpopular with motorbike owners.
What these debates reveal is that a pavement is never just infrastructure. It reflects a society's assumptions about who has the right to public space and for what purpose. In cities where many people live in cramped homes, the street functions as an extension of the living room — and any policy that ignores this is likely to fail, however tidy it looks on paper.

qs.q: What criticism is made of 'reclaim the pavement' campaigns?
qs.a: They mainly affect poor vendors rather than big businesses
w: They make the streets more dangerous
They are too expensive to run
qs.why: “tend to target the poorest… while leaving untouched the cafés and car showrooms.”

qs.q: What do urban planners suggest?
qs.a: Finding ways for walking and trade to share space
qs.why: “they suggest asking how both can coexist.”

qs.q: Why, according to the writer, is the street like a living room for some residents?
qs.why: “In cities where many people live in cramped homes, the street functions as an extension of the living room.”

qs.q: What does 'however tidy it looks on paper' imply?
qs.a: A plan may seem good in theory but fail in reality
w: Plans should be written more carefully
qs.why: Câu nói chính sách bỏ qua thực tế sẽ thất bại dù trên giấy trông gọn gàng.

items.title: The Value of Boredom
items.tvi: Giá trị của sự buồn chán
items.text:
Boredom has a poor reputation. We associate it with wasted time, restless children and endless meetings, and we have built an entire industry — from streaming services to infinite social media feeds — dedicated to ensuring we never have to experience it. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that this may be a mistake.
In one frequently cited study, participants were first given a deliberately tedious task: copying numbers from a telephone directory. Afterwards, they were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had been bored came up with significantly more creative ideas than a control group who had gone straight to the second task. The researchers concluded that boredom may push the mind to search for stimulation internally, encouraging the kind of wandering thought from which original ideas emerge.
There is also a motivational dimension. Boredom, some argue, is essentially a signal that our current activity lacks meaning, prompting us to look for something more worthwhile. If we immediately silence that signal by reaching for a phone, we may never ask whether we should be doing something different with our lives.
This is not an argument for embracing tedium for its own sake. Chronic boredom, particularly in work or school, is associated with poorer performance and even health problems. The point is rather that brief, unstructured moments — waiting for a bus, lying awake, staring out of a window — may be more valuable than we assume. Filling every one of them with entertainment could, paradoxically, leave us with less to think about.

qs.q: What did the study with plastic cups suggest?
qs.a: Being bored first can increase creativity
w: Boring tasks make people less creative
qs.why: “Those who had been bored came up with significantly more creative ideas.”

qs.q: According to the 'motivational' argument, what is boredom a sign of?
qs.a: That what we are doing lacks meaning
qs.why: “Boredom… is essentially a signal that our current activity lacks meaning.”

qs.q: What does the writer say about long-term boredom?
qs.why: “Chronic boredom… is associated with poorer performance and even health problems.”

qs.q: What is the 'paradox' in the final sentence?
qs.a: Constant entertainment may reduce our thinking
w: Boredom is both good and fun
Waiting for a bus is entertaining
qs.why: “Filling every one of them with entertainment could, paradoxically, leave us with less to think about.”

items.title: Translating Poetry
items.text:
It is often said that poetry is what gets lost in translation. The remark is usually attributed to Robert Frost, although there is little evidence he ever said it, which is itself a small lesson in how ideas travel and change.
The difficulty is obvious to anyone who has tried. A poem is not simply a set of meanings; it is a particular arrangement of sounds, rhythms and associations, many of which are unique to the language in which it was written. Vietnamese, with its six tones, allows effects of musicality that English cannot reproduce. Conversely, English poets exploit rhyme and stress patterns that have no Vietnamese equivalent. A translator must therefore decide, line by line, what to sacrifice.
Some translators prioritise literal accuracy, producing versions that are faithful but often flat. Others aim to recreate the effect of the original, accepting that this may require substantial changes to its words. The poet and translator Huynh Sanh Thong, for instance, chose to render 'The Tale of Kieu' in English verse, accepting losses in precision in exchange for a work that could be read as poetry in its own right.
Critics have long debated which approach is superior, but the question may be unanswerable. Each translation is an interpretation, and a great poem can sustain many. Indeed, comparing several translations of the same work can reveal aspects of the original that no single version captures. Seen this way, translation is less a matter of loss than of multiplication: the poem survives not in one perfect copy, but in many imperfect ones.

qs.q: What point does the writer make about the Robert Frost quotation?
qs.a: It may not be his, showing how ideas change as they spread
w: It proves poetry cannot be translated
It was first written in Vietnamese
qs.why: “there is little evidence he ever said it, which is itself a small lesson in how ideas travel and change.”

qs.q: Why is poetry especially hard to translate?
qs.a: It depends on sound and associations specific to a language
w: Poets use too many rare words
qs.why: “a particular arrangement of sounds, rhythms and associations, many of which are unique to the language.”

qs.q: What did Huynh Sanh Thong accept in his translation?
qs.a: Less precision in return for a poetic English version
qs.why: “accepting losses in precision in exchange for a work that could be read as poetry in its own right.”

qs.q: What is the writer's final view of translation?
qs.a: Multiple translations together enrich our understanding
w: Only one translation can be correct
qs.why: “translation is less a matter of loss than of multiplication.”

items.title: Rewilding: Letting Nature Take Over
items.tvi: Tái hoang dã: để thiên nhiên tự phục hồi
items.text:
For much of the twentieth century, conservation meant carefully managing landscapes: cutting back vegetation, controlling animal populations and preserving particular habitats in a fixed state. Over the past two decades, an alternative philosophy known as rewilding has gained ground. Its central idea is that, given space and time, natural processes will restore damaged ecosystems more effectively than human intervention.
In practice, rewilding often involves removing barriers rather than adding things — taking down fences, allowing rivers to flood, or ending intensive farming on marginal land. In some projects, missing species are reintroduced. The return of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the United States is the most famous example: by reducing the number of deer that grazed along riverbanks, the wolves allowed trees to recover, which in turn stabilised the banks and created habitats for birds and fish.
The approach is not without controversy. Farmers fear that predators will attack livestock, and some rural communities resent what they see as outsiders deciding the future of their land. Ecologists themselves disagree about how far 'wildness' is achievable in densely populated regions, where human influence is unavoidable.
Advocates respond that rewilding need not mean excluding people. Several projects in Europe have created jobs in eco-tourism that replace income lost from farming. The challenge, they argue, is less ecological than social: persuading communities that a landscape left partly to itself can still be a source of livelihood and pride.

qs.q: How does rewilding differ from traditional conservation?
qs.a: It relies on natural processes instead of close management
w: It focuses on protecting single species
It requires more fences and barriers
qs.why: “natural processes will restore damaged ecosystems more effectively than human intervention.”

qs.q: How did wolves help the rivers in Yellowstone?
qs.a: They reduced deer, so trees recovered along the banks
w: They ate fish that damaged the banks
They kept people away from the rivers
qs.why: “by reducing the number of deer… the wolves allowed trees to recover, which in turn stabilised the banks.”

qs.q: Why do some rural communities oppose rewilding?
qs.a: They feel others are deciding about their land
qs.why: “some rural communities resent what they see as outsiders deciding the future of their land.”

qs.q: According to advocates, what is the main challenge?
qs.a: Convincing local people of its benefits
qs.why: “The challenge… is less ecological than social: persuading communities…”

items.title: The Ethics of Tipping
items.tvi: Chuyện đạo đức của tiền boa
items.text:
Few social customs vary as widely between countries as tipping. In the United States, failing to leave around twenty percent in a restaurant is considered a serious insult, since many waiting staff depend on tips for most of their income. In Japan, by contrast, offering a tip can cause genuine confusion, as good service is regarded as part of the job rather than a favour deserving extra payment. Vietnam sits somewhere in between: tipping is not expected in most local restaurants but has become common in hotels and tourist venues.
Defenders of tipping argue that it rewards effort and gives customers a way to express appreciation. Yet research casts doubt on the idea that tips reflect service quality. Studies have found that the size of a tip is influenced far more by factors such as the weather, the size of the bill and whether the server introduced themselves by name than by how well the customer was actually served. More troublingly, several studies have found evidence that tips can be affected by the server's appearance, age or ethnicity.
Critics therefore argue that tipping shifts responsibility for fair wages from employers to customers, while exposing workers to income that is unpredictable and, at times, discriminatory. Some restaurants have experimented with 'no-tipping' policies, raising menu prices and paying staff a higher fixed wage instead. Results have been mixed: staff welcome the stability, but some customers react badly to the higher prices on the menu, even when the total cost is the same.
The persistence of tipping, in other words, may have less to do with economics than with psychology.

qs.q: Why might a tip cause confusion in Japan?
qs.a: Good service is seen as a normal part of the job
qs.why: “good service is regarded as part of the job rather than a favour deserving extra payment.”

qs.q: What does research say about tips and service quality?
qs.a: Tips depend more on other factors than on service

items.title: Why Do We Keep Things We Never Use?
items.tvi: Vì sao ta giữ đồ không bao giờ dùng?
items.text:
Open almost any cupboard and you will find them: cables for devices that no longer exist, clothes that have not fitted for years, kitchen gadgets used once and then forgotten. Most of us accept that we own too much, yet getting rid of things is surprisingly difficult. Behavioural economists offer several explanations.
The first is the so-called endowment effect: people tend to value an object more highly simply because they own it. In classic experiments, participants given a coffee mug demanded roughly twice as much to sell it as other participants were willing to pay to buy the same mug. Ownership, it seems, changes our perception of worth.
A second factor is the fear of future regret. Throwing something away closes off a possibility — the chance that we might need it one day — and the imagined pain of regretting that decision often outweighs the small, steady inconvenience of clutter. This helps explain why people keep items 'just in case' long after any realistic case has passed.
Finally, objects are often bound up with identity and memory. A worn-out jacket may represent a period of one's life; discarding it can feel like discarding part of oneself. Professional organisers report that clients frequently find it easier to let go of an item after taking a photograph of it, preserving the memory without the object.
Understanding these biases does not make decluttering painless, but it may make it more manageable. Recognising that our attachment is, at least partly, an illusion created by ownership can make the decision to let go feel less like a loss.

qs.a: Owners valued the mug more than potential buyers did
w: People prefer new mugs to old ones
Buyers would pay double the shop price
qs.why: “participants given a coffee mug demanded roughly twice as much to sell it as other participants were willing to pay.”

qs.q: Why do people keep things 'just in case'?
qs.a: They fear regretting throwing them away
w: They plan to sell them later
qs.why: “the imagined pain of regretting that decision often outweighs the small, steady inconvenience of clutter.”

qs.q: Why do organisers suggest taking a photograph?
qs.a: It keeps the memory while the object goes
w: It helps sell the item online
It shows how much clutter there is
qs.why: “preserving the memory without the object.”

qs.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
qs.a: Understanding our biases can make decluttering easier
w: People should never throw things away
qs.why: “Understanding these biases does not make decluttering painless, but it may make it more manageable.”

items.title: The Rise of the Remote Village
items.text:
When high-speed internet reached the small coastal town of Quy Nhon's surrounding villages, few predicted that it would attract software developers, designers and writers from Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. Yet over the past three years, dozens of so-called 'digital nomads' have settled there, drawn by low rents, clean air and the possibility of working for city clients while living by the sea.
Local reactions have been mixed. Guesthouse owners and café proprietors welcome the steady year-round income, which offsets the seasonal swings of tourism. Some young people who had planned to leave for the city have stayed, finding work in services that cater to the newcomers. On the other hand, rents in the most popular areas have risen sharply, and some long-term residents complain that they are being priced out of their own neighbourhoods.
There are also subtler tensions. Newcomers often keep city hours and socialise mainly with one another, creating what one resident called 'a village inside the village'. Their incomes, earned elsewhere, can be several times the local average, a disparity that is visible in everything from the cars they drive to the restaurants they frequent.
Sociologists studying similar trends elsewhere caution against simple judgements. Remote workers can revitalise declining rural economies, but the benefits are rarely shared evenly unless local authorities intervene — for instance, by protecting affordable housing or encouraging newcomers to employ local staff. Whether Quy Nhon's villages become a model of balanced growth or a cautionary tale, they suggest, will depend less on the internet than on the choices made by the people living there.

qs.a: They provide income throughout the year
w: They bring tourists in the summer
qs.why: “welcome the steady year-round income, which offsets the seasonal swings of tourism.”
